body.text: SR&ED subcontractor costs are amounts a Canadian claimant pays contractors to perform scientific research and experimental development in Canada on its behalf. Under the Income Tax Act, 100% of an arm's-length taxable supplier's contract enters the Section 37 deduction pool, but only 80% qualifies for the federal investment tax credit.

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is the federal government's largest single source of financial support for industrial innovation, distributing approximately $4.5 billion annually in investment tax credits (ITCs) according to industry funding analyses, alongside immediate or carryforward income tax deductions. Governed jointly by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates legislative tax policy) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA, which administers technical and financial compliance), the statutory regime operates through two primary mechanisms under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)): an immediate and indefinitely carryforwardable deduction pool for allowable SR&ED expenditures under Section 37, and a tax credit regime under Sections 127 and 127.1 that provides either a 15% basic rate or an enhanced 35% refundable rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most expansive structural reform in over a decade. Following policy announcements in the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement, draft legislative proposals released by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025, and further enhancements tabled by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne, in the November 4, 2025 federal budget, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, these legislative amendments doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED ITC from $3 million to $6 million (allowing up to $2.1 million annually in refundable federal credits), raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an alternative three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure ($15 million–$75 million), extended access to the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, at the provincial level, Quebec abolished eight legacy R&D tax credit measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating them into the fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% credit on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess spending.

For corporate tax directors, R&D auditors, and legal counsel, navigating the post-Bill C-15 regime requires strict separation between the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool. An expenditure may be fully deductible under Section 37 while generating a reduced, partially refundable, or nil ITC under Section 127—such as used depreciable capital equipment (100% deductible under Paragraph 37(1)(b), 0% eligible for ITC under Regulation 2902(b)), arm's-length Canadian subcontractor payments (100% deductible under Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), 80% eligible for ITC under Subsection 127(9)), or the Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% of the capped direct SR&ED salary base under Regulation 2900(4), which earns an ITC under Section 127 but is never added to the Section 37 deduction pool). Furthermore, all claims remain subject to a strict, non-extendable statutory reporting deadline of 12 months after the income tax return filing-due date (18 months after the corporate taxation year-end) under Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m), alongside rigorous contemporaneous documentation standards shaped by Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence.
1. Executive Summary of the 2025–2026 SR&ED Legislative Reforms

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 fundamentally recalibrated the economics of conducting industrial research and experimental development in Canada. Prior to the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the federal SR&ED regime had remained largely static since the 2012 federal budget reforms (which took effect in 2013 and 2014), when Parliament eliminated capital expenditure and capital lease eligibility, reduced the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rate from 65% to 55%, and restricted arm's-length contract expenditures to 80% for ITC purposes.

The legislative progression of the 2024–2026 reforms occurred in three distinct stages that tax practitioners must track carefully when auditing working papers prepared during the transition period. First, the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement—released as formal draft legislative proposals and explanatory notes by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025—initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million (yielding a maximum refundable credit of $1.575 million), expanding the taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a consolidated gross revenue phase-out test, and restoring capital expenditure and lease cost eligibility for property acquired or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024. Second, on November 4, 2025, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne, presented the 2025 federal budget, which confirmed all structural measures from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and further increased the annual SR&ED expenditure limit from the proposed $4.5 million to $6 million, retroactively effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Third, Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, codifying the $6 million expenditure limit and all associated amendments to Sections 37, 127, and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act. Following Royal Assent, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval program on April 1, 2026, released updated versions of Form T661, Form T1145, and Form T1146 on May 15, 2026, updated T2 Schedule 31 on May 22, 2026, updated T2 Schedule 49 on May 29, 2026, and issued revised administrative policies for Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and Lease Expenditures in May and June 2026.

body.text: 2. Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of Eligibility (Subsection 248(1))
2.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED

The legal foundation for all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada (including Quebec’s harmonized R&D definition under the CRIC) is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in Subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act. What is colloquially referred to in industry or financial accounting as "research and development" (R&D) does not automatically constitute SR&ED for Canadian tax purposes. To qualify, work must strictly satisfy the opening preamble of Subsection 248(1), fall within one of the three core categories in Paragraphs (a) through (c) (or qualify as commensurate support work under Paragraph (d)), and avoid the seven statutory exclusions in Paragraphs (e) through (k).

Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statute divides eligible core research into three categories: Paragraph (a) basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view (for example, investigating the fundamental molecular characteristics of a newly discovered virus to expand the existing scientific knowledge base); Paragraph (b) applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view (for example, conducting scientific investigations to develop a vaccine targeting a virus based on its newly identified molecular properties); and Paragraph (c) experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development is the most frequently claimed category in Canadian industrial claims. In addition, Paragraph (d) support work encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in Paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, Subsection 248(1) explicitly stipulates that SR&ED does not include work with respect to any of seven excluded categories (collectively referred to as the statutory exclusions in Paragraphs (e) through (k)). These excluded activities are: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection. Carrying out activities that fall within Paragraphs (e) to (k) does not taint or disqualify concurrent SR&ED work on the same commercial initiative, provided the excluded work is properly segregated and omitted from the SR&ED claim.
2.2 Evolution of Administrative Guidance: From IC 86-4R3 and the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Framework

Understanding how the CRA audits technical eligibility requires tracing the doctrinal evolution of the agency's administrative guidelines. Prior to 1985, Revenue Canada administered R&D incentives under Interpretation Bulletin IT-439. Following taxpayer feedback that IT-439 failed to explain the boundaries of eligible industrial development, the Department of Finance tabled the May 23, 1985 Budget Papers (Securing Economic Renewal), introducing the statutory term "experimental development" to confirm that projects involving only routine engineering or routine development are excluded. On March 4, 1986, in response to Revenue Canada's request for clarification, the Department of Finance confirmed that eligible activities must embody three core criteria: scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and systematic and organized investigation advancing the understanding of scientific or technological relationships. Revenue Canada and industry leaders co-developed Information Circular IC 86-4 in 1986 (revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994), followed by Government of Canada News Release 92-088 on December 2, 1992, which emphasized that the purpose of experimental development must be achieving technological advancement to create or improve materials, devices, products, or processes.

In 1998, Judge Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada synthesized IC 86-4R3 and Subsection 248(1) in the landmark decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839), establishing a five-question judicial approach. The CRA formally codified those five questions in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012 and revised in 2015), asking: (1) whether there was a scientific or technological uncertainty; (2) whether the effort involved formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; (3) whether the overall approach adopted was consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis; (4) whether the overall approach was undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement; and (5) whether a record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed.

On August 13, 2021, following a 2020 modernization review, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and published the current Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. The 2021 Guidelines consolidated the five questions into two overarching statutory requirements derived directly from Subsection 248(1)—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement. As the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88), the 2021 Guidelines did not alter the substantive law; rather, the "Why" and "How" requirements encapsulate the exact same five common-law elements established in Northwest Hydraulic.
2.3 Detailed Analysis of the "Why" and "How" Requirements
The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty)

The "Why" requirement examines the underlying purpose of the work: it must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The CRA distinguishes between generating conceptual knowledge (new theories, explanatory frameworks, or prediction models) and purely factual knowledge (routine data or measurements). Categorizing knowledge as either scientific or technological is not critical, as both are eligible.

New scientific or technological knowledge is needed only when the claimant encounters a scientific or technological uncertainty—defined as an insufficiency or limitation in the available base of scientific or technological knowledge such that it is unknown or uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, using available knowledge and standard practice. Available knowledge encompasses both the internal technical resources of the claimant's business environment (considering business size, industry sector, competition, and access to technical expertise) and all publicly accessible sources known to competent professionals in the field. Resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty constitutes an attempt to achieve scientific or technological advancement.

The CRA's guidelines identify seven specific characteristics of technical problems that suggest the available technological knowledge base is insufficient: (1) existing design methods are not applicable; (2) requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; (3) there are too many variables or unknowns; (4) parameters or conditions lie outside the normal operating range; (5) the nature of the problem is evolving; (6) data is not readily available; or (7) interlocking constraints exist.

Three vital legal boundary rules govern the "Why" requirement. First, success or failure in meeting technical or commercial objectives is irrelevant when assessing the "Why" requirement, because Subsection 248(1) only requires that the purpose of the work be for achieving scientific or technological advancement; proving through systematic experimentation why a hypothesis failed advances the technological knowledge base. Second, workarounds are ineligible: circumventing an uncertainty using available knowledge without attempting to resolve the underlying uncertainty renders the work ineligible. Third, acquiring existing knowledge and purely economic targets do not qualify on their own: acquiring available know-how through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not attempt to achieve technological advancement, and cost targets alone do not create technological uncertainty unless attempting to achieve target costs under technical constraints gives rise to technological uncertainty.
The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

Following standard design methods or systematic problem-solving approaches is not sufficient on its own to satisfy the "How" requirement. Under Subsection 248(1) and CRA guidelines, a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis must incorporate four sequential elements:

items: Generating an Idea or Hypothesis: Formulating an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving the objective or resolving the problem, expressed as a possible solution, proposed method, or approach.
Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the idea to evolve and change as a result of testing.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Formulating logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis.
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Preserving evidence and records of the hypotheses tested and results obtained as the work progresses.

body.text: 2.4 Distinguishing Support Work from Excluded Work and Shop-Floor Boundaries

Under Paragraph 248(1)(d), the eight enumerated categories of support work—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research—are never SR&ED on their own. They qualify only when they are commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada. Because activities like "testing" and "data collection" appear both in Paragraph (d) (eligible support work) and in Paragraphs (f) and (k) (excluded routine testing and routine data collection), the CRA differentiates them strictly by purpose. If data collection or testing is performed as a routine activity supporting normal business operations (such as quality control or assurance), it is excluded under Paragraph (f) or (k), whereas if it is carried out specifically to directly support scientific research or experimental development, it qualifies as eligible support work under Paragraph (d).

Similarly, under the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, the CRA distinguishes between a Company Project (which has a commercial purpose, such as product line expansion, facility construction, or process upgrades) and an SR&ED Project (the subset of interrelated activities collectively necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties through systematic investigation by qualified individuals). An SR&ED project commences when scientific or technological uncertainties are identified and technical objectives are established (including necessary preliminary technical feasibility studies, provided they are followed up with experimental testing or analysis) and concludes when the uncertainty is resolved, determined to be unresolvable, or the project is terminated. Troubleshooting, debugging, fine-tuning without technical uncertainty, and customer-site implementation or beta testing to verify customer specifications are excluded under Paragraph (i).
3. Section 37 Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool Mechanics
3.1 The Subsection 37(1) Running Pool Calculation

The first pillar of the federal SR&ED incentive is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures governed by Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act. Allowable current and post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada are accumulated in a running tax pool that allows immediate or indefinitely deferred deduction against business income. To qualify for inclusion in the Subsection 37(1) pool, the expenditures must be incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada (including Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone under Subsection 37(1.3)) and must be related to a business carried on by the taxpayer—or, where the claimant is a corporation, related to a business actively engaged in by a related corporation under Subsection 37(1.1) (such as a parent corporation actively engaged in business while a subsidiary performs the SR&ED).

At the end of each taxation year, the available balance in the Subsection 37(1) pool (calculated in Part 3 of Form T661) is determined by adding current-year increases to the prior-year unamortized pool balance and subtracting statutory reductions:

body.text: 3.2 Permissive Deduction, Indefinite Carryforward, Negative Balances, and Loss Restriction Events

Once the year-end Subsection 37(1) pool balance is determined, four structural tax planning rules govern its utilization. First, for corporations and sole proprietors, claiming a deduction from the Subsection 37(1) pool on T2 Schedule 1 (Line 411) is optional (permissive). A claimant may choose to deduct all, a portion, or none of the available positive pool balance in calculating business income for a taxation year, and any undeducted positive balance does not expire—it carries forward indefinitely to be deducted in any subsequent taxation year. Moreover, while identifying SR&ED expenditures into the pool is bound by the 18-month Form T661 reporting deadline under Subsection 37(11), the subsequent deduction of an already-pooled balance on Schedule 1 is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline. Second, under Paragraph 96(1)(e.1), a partnership is prohibited from carrying forward an amount in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent year; the pool balance at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be deducted in full when computing the partnership's net income for that year.

Third, if a negative balance arises in the Subsection 37(1) pool at the end of a taxation year (typically because Paragraph 37(1)(e) reductions for prior-year federal ITCs refunded or applied exceed current-year additions and opening pool balances), that negative balance must be brought into net business income for tax purposes in that year under Paragraph 12(1)(v). The amount included in income under Paragraph 12(1)(v) is then added back to the pool in the following taxation year under Paragraph 37(1)(c.1) so that the opening pool balance resets to nil ($0). Fourth, when control of a corporation is acquired or a trust acquires a new majority-interest beneficiary (a "loss restriction event"), Paragraph 37(1)(h) and Subsection 37(6.1) reduce the unrestricted pool balance to nil and restrict the carryforward of unused pre-acquisition SR&ED pool balances (including capital expenditures made or acquired on or after December 16, 2024 under amended Clause 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B)). Additionally, under Subsection 37(4) and Regulation 2902(c), no deduction is ever allowed for an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED, and Subsection 37(5) denies an SR&ED deduction where an amount is claimed as a corporate or charitable gift under Section 110.1 or Section 118.1.
4. Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Mechanics
4.1 Basic (15%) vs. Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates

The second pillar of the federal SR&ED program is the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) governed by Section 127 (specifically Subsections 127(5), 127(8), 127(9), 127(10.1), 127(10.3), 127(10.5), and 127(10.64)) and Section 127.1 (which governs cash refundability). Unlike the Section 37 deduction pool, the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" defined in Subsection 127(9) is calculated at the end of each taxation year and does not carry over to another taxation year; instead, it generates current-year ITCs. Note that under Subsection 127(9), no amount is considered an ITC if any of the claimant's income from the business is exempt from Part I tax.

Under Paragraph 127(9)(a.1), the basic SR&ED ITC rate is 15% of the amount by which the taxpayer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year exceeds the total of all provincial super-allowance benefit amounts for the year. This 15% basic rate applies to: (a) corporations that do not qualify as a CCPC or an ECPC (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries or large Canadian public corporations exceeding the phase-out ceiling); (b) qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs on the portion of their annual qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their annual expenditure limit; and (c) sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership (allocated via Subsection 127(8)), and beneficiaries of trusts.

Under Subsection 127(10.1), eligible corporations earn a 20% enhancement over the 15% basic rate—yielding an enhanced SR&ED ITC rate of 35%—on their qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, only Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs, as defined in Subsection 125(7)) could earn the 35% rate up to a maximum expenditure limit of $3,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 increased the maximum expenditure limit to $6,000,000 (generating up to $2,100,000 in enhanced ITCs per year) and expanded eligibility to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).
4.2 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and CCPC De-Association Relief

Under the definition added to Subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) is a corporation that, throughout the taxation year, meets three statutory criteria: (1) it is resident in Canada; (2) a class of its shares is listed on a designated stock exchange (or it has elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) it is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. In addition, under the "eligible subsidiary" definition in Subsection 127(9), a Canadian-resident corporation in which not less than 90% (all or substantially all) of the issued shares of each class of capital stock are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more ECPCs is also eligible to access the enhanced 35% refundable ITC.

For private start-ups backed by venture capital or angel syndicates, the Income Tax Act also contains de-association relief provisions. Under normal corporate association rules, if two otherwise unassociated corporations are associated with the same third corporation, or if the same group of unconnected investors owns shares in multiple CCPCs, those CCPCs could be considered associated and forced to share a single expenditure limit. To ensure small businesses are not hindered when venture capital investors invest in multiple portfolio companies, the relieving provisions in Section 127 deem corporations not to be associated for purposes of calculating the expenditure limit and refundable ITC if the only reason they would be associated is that two or more investors own shares in each corporation, provided there is at least one shareholder of one of the corporations who is not a shareholder of the other corporation and the existence of that shareholder is not for the purpose of satisfying the relief provisions.
4.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Consolidated Gross Revenue

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit (which must be allocated among associated CCPCs on T2 Schedule 49 under Subsection 127(10.3), or among members of a consolidated group for ECPCs under Subsection 127(10.64)) is subject to two distinct phase-out methods:
Method A: Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out (Default for CCPCs)

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit phased out based on prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 (using the qualifying income limit formula $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000]). Under the post-December 15, 2024 rules enacted by Bill C-15, the gradual reduction of the expenditure limit for a CCPC (on an associated basis) begins when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $15,000,000 and is completely eliminated at $75,000,000 (updating the qualifying income limit formula to $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,000, up to $60,000,000). Under the initial $4,500,000 expenditure limit proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, this $60,000,000 phase-out span equated to a straight-line reduction of $0.075 per $1.00 of taxable capital above $15,000,000; under the enacted $6,000,000 expenditure limit from the November 4, 2025 federal budget, the $6,000,000 limit phases out proportionally over the same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 ($60,000,000) range ($0.10 per $1.00 of taxable capital above $15,000,000). Corporations with prior-year taxable capital of $75,000,000 or more have a nil expenditure limit and claim the non-refundable federal ITC at the 15% basic rate.
Method B: Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs)

For an ECPC, the expenditure limit is phased out based on its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years ending in the last calendar year that ended before the end of the particular taxation year, as reflected in annual financial statements prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) and presented to shareholders (at the highest level of consolidation if the ECPC is a member of a "consolidated group" with an Ultimate Parent Entity under Subsection 127(9)). Mirroring the taxable capital thresholds, the expenditure limit phases out on a straight-line basis when three-year average annual gross revenue is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 ($0.075 per $1.00 under the $4.5M FES proposal; $0.10 per $1.00 under the enacted $6.0M limit), becoming fully eliminated at $75,000,000.

Crucially, a CCPC may elect on a year-by-year basis (using the prescribed form) to have its expenditure limit determined using this three-year average gross revenue structure instead of the prior-year taxable capital structure, allowing each CCPC to choose whichever method yields the higher expenditure limit for that taxation year. Under Subsection 127(10.64), specific proration and annualization rules apply to consolidated groups and short periods: Paragraph 127(10.64)(a) parallels the associated CCPC allocation rules for members of a consolidated group; Paragraph 127(10.64)(b) requires prorating an ECPC's expenditure limit for a short taxation year (fewer than 51 weeks) by multiplying by the number of days in the taxation year and dividing by 365 (paralleling Subsection 127(10.5) for CCPCs); Paragraphs 127(10.64)(c) and (d) require a "gross up" of financial statement revenue for any short fiscal year (fewer than 51 weeks) in the three-year lookback period by multiplying by 365 and dividing by the number of days in that fiscal year; and Paragraph 127(10.64)(e) provides that where fewer than three preceding fiscal years exist, average annual revenue is calculated over the actual number of completed fiscal years (one or two fiscal years).
4.4 Section 127.1 Refundability Matrix, Carrybacks, and Carryforwards

Whether an SR&ED ITC results in a cash refund under Section 127.1 or remains a non-refundable credit used to offset Part I federal income tax payable depends on the claimant's legal status, whether the expenditures fall within the expenditure limit, and whether the expenditures are current or capital in nature. body.text: Mechanics of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4) to (10)

When a taxpayer elects the Proxy Method on Line 160, it foregoes claiming actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures (such as travel, training, property taxes, maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment, and office supplies). Instead, under Subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the taxpayer computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of its SR&ED Salary Base (calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 on Line 818, multiplied by 55% on Line 820, and entered on Line 502 of Part 4).

Computing the Salary Base (Line 818 = Line 814 + Line 816) requires strict compliance with Regulations 2900(7), 2900(8), 2900(9), and 2900(10). Under Regulation 2900(9), for all employees (whether specified or non-specified), the salary base must exclude: (1) taxable benefits under Section 6; (2) stock option benefits under Section 7; (3) unpaid amounts from a prior year paid in the current taxation year (Line 310); (4) remuneration based on profits; (5) bonuses; and (6) employer contributions to related benefits. For non-specified employees, the total direct SR&ED wages from Lines 300 and 307 are entered on Line 810, the excluded bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits are subtracted on Line 812, and the net eligible salary base is entered on Line 814.

For each specified employee (an employee who owns, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or a related corporation, or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation), Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8) restrict the amount included in the Part 5 Salary Base (Line 816, summed from Column 6 / Box 860 of Table 7) to the lesser of two statutory ceilings. The first ceiling is Box 856 (the 75% Time Cap), which multiplies 100% of the specified employee's total base salary or wages for the year across both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and Line 310 amounts, entered in Box 852) by the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED, subject to a maximum cap of 75% (Box 854). The second ceiling is Box 858 (the 2.5 × YMPE Limit), calculated using the formula 2.5 × A × B ÷ 365, where A is the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the corporation employed the individual. Under Regulation 2900(8) and (10), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in the same calendar year, the combined salary base inclusion across all associated corporations cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE.

Furthermore, Regulation 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA to ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed the total business expenditures made in the taxation year. The Overall Cap is calculated as A − B − C, where A is total amounts deducted in computing net business income for tax purposes for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of deductions claimed in the year under Sections 20 (such as CCA, interest, and bad debts), 24 (ceasing business), 26 (banks), 30 (farming land improvements), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED pool deduction on Schedule 1 Line 411), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts); and C is expenditures incurred for the use of, or right to use, a building (building rent). In practice, the Overall Cap does not restrict the 55% PPA so long as the claimant deducts more than $55 of non-SR&ED, non-rent operating expenses for each $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.
Mechanics of the Traditional Method Overhead Test (Regulation 2900(2)(c))

If a claimant elects the Traditional Method on Line 162, it may claim overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 only if each expenditure (or reasonably allocated portion thereof) satisfies the two-part "directly attributable" test under Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations. First, under the Directly Related Test, the expenditure must have a direct linkage—with no intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED in Canada. For example, a Personnel Manager directly hiring SR&ED staff meets the directly related test, whereas a Vice-President hiring that Personnel Manager involves an intervening step and does not qualify. Second, under the Incremental Test, the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Variable costs that vary in direct relation to usage or production (such as electricity, gas, water, or variable equipment operating and repair costs) can have an incremental percentage claimed, whereas a fixed cost that does not vary with increases or decreases in usage (such as a fixed-cost annual maintenance contract) fails the incremental test and cannot be claimed. Headhunter/recruiter fees, job advertising, interview travel, and immigration/work permit costs for selecting SR&ED personnel are deductible only as regular business expenses, whereas moving expenses to relocate hired hands-on SR&ED personnel to a Canadian facility and related employee taxable benefits (such as housing loss benefits) are allowable SR&ED overhead.
5.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employee Caps, and CPP YMPE Benchmarks

Under Subsection 37(8), Paragraph 2900(2)(b) of the Regulations, and the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, employee remuneration (defined in Subsection 248(1) as employment income under Sections 5 to 8, excluding pension/superannuation benefits and retiring allowances) is segregated on Form T661 into employees other than specified employees (Line 300 for work in Canada; Line 307 for permissible work outside Canada) and specified employees (Line 305 for work in Canada; Line 309 for permissible work outside Canada).

Only the proportion of time an employee spends directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED tasks qualifies on Lines 300–309, determined strictly by actual tasks performed rather than job titles. Qualifying directly engaged tasks include: preparing equipment and materials for experiments, tests, and analyses (excluding equipment maintenance); carrying out experiments, tests, and analyses; collecting data, recording measurements, making calculations, and preparing charts and graphs directly supporting experimentation; carrying out required statistical surveys and interviews; preparing computer programs, engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, and psychological research required for an SR&ED project; and first-line supervision by managers or supervisors who direct the technical course of ongoing SR&ED or provide direct technical input into the work. Work performed beyond the first-line level of supervision, non-technological management decision-making, equipment maintenance, and clerical or administrative services (accounting, payroll, finance, legal support, purchasing, sales, human resources, shipping, inventory control, word processing) do not qualify as directly engaged work. Under Regulation 2900(5), if an employee performs directly engaged SR&ED duties all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of their time, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is included.

For non-specified employees (Line 300), allowable salary or wages include base pay, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay (excluding extended vacation or sick leave), pay in lieu of termination notice, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and cash outlays for Section 6 taxable benefits (or non-cash taxable benefits if the value is a reasonable estimate of actual cost excluding recoverable GST/HST/PST and actual costs are not claimed elsewhere). Stock option benefits under Section 7 and the employer's share of related payroll benefits are excluded from direct wages.

For specified employees on Line 305, three strict statutory limitations apply: (1) bonuses and remuneration based on profits must be completely excluded; (2) the maximum amount of direct SR&ED salary or wages claimed on Line 305 is capped at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (5 × YMPE) determined for purposes of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the employee was a specified employee; and (3) if the specified employee performs SR&ED for associated corporations, the 5 × YMPE maximum must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development) under Subsection 37(9.3).

Because Canada introduced the second additional Canada Pension Plan contribution ceiling (CPP2)—known as the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE)—beginning January 1, 2024, auditors must verify that SR&ED specified employee calculations use the first earnings ceiling (the YMPE under Section 18 of the CPP) and not the higher YAMPE. body.text: Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.5) and 37(2))

While contract work performed outside Canada never qualifies for SR&ED tax incentives (being deductible only as an ordinary business expense), Subsections 37(1.5) and 37(2) permit a claimant to include permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada (Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661) up to the lesser of Amount A and Amount B. Amount A comprises salaries or wages for SR&ED work outside Canada that was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (not a contractor) who was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred, where the work was directly related to a business of the claimant and was solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant. Amount B caps the claim at 10% of the total eligible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on in Canada (Lines 300 + 305) in that taxation year.
Unpaid Remuneration and Unpaid Current Expenditures (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))

Under Subsection 78(4) (for employee remuneration, reported on Line 315) and Subsection 127(26) (for other current SR&ED expenditures, reported on Line 520), any SR&ED expenditure incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year, and is instead treated as incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. Under Paragraph 127(9)(m), unpaid amounts must be identified on Form T661 within the original 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for the year the expense was accrued; if an unpaid amount is not identified on time, it can never be included in calculating total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes, even when paid in a future year. For an unpaid arm's-length SR&ED contract expenditure, the claimant reports only 80% of the unpaid contract amount on Line 520, and adds back only 80% of the amount paid on the prior-year unpaid amounts line in the year of payment.
5.3 Materials Consumed (Line 320) vs. Materials Transformed (Line 325)

Under Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (B)(V), Paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, and the Materials for SR&ED Policy, a claimant may claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in performing SR&ED in Canada under both the Proxy and Traditional methods. "Materials for SR&ED" must be physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or items (generally in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is carried out or that results from the SR&ED (including intermediate products, by-products, final products, or test animals and plants, though excluding unmanipulated control groups in commercial production settings and limiting agricultural inputs like feed, fertilizer, and pesticides during commercial production runs to incremental costs).

Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials used up, destroyed, or rendered unusable during the prosecution of SR&ED (such as cardboard boxes destroyed during experimental printing trials that have no resale value). Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials or component parts changed in character or form or incorporated into another tangible product or asset that has some value to either the claimant or another party. The claimable amount is the laid-down cost, which includes invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, storage costs, and preparatory third-party service costs (such as galvanizing metal parts prior to testing), or the production/industrial cost price (including a proper share of production overhead, even under the Proxy Method) for internally manufactured inventory. Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED—never when merely received from a supplier, manufactured without experimental development, or removed from inventory. Under Subsection 127(11.6), if materials are purchased from a non-arm's-length supplier, the ITC is restricted to the actual cost incurred by the non-arm's-length supplier, excluding any intercompany profit markup (adjusted on Line 543).
5.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers (Form T1146), and Third-Party Payments (Form T1263)
Payments to external parties for SR&ED are governed by three distinct statutory regimes on Form T661:
1. Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340, Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01))

Where a claimant pays an arm's-length performer that is a "taxable supplier" (a Canadian resident or a non-resident carrying on business through a Canadian permanent establishment) to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool, but under Subparagraph 127(9) "qualified expenditure" (a)(ii), only 80% of the expenditure qualifies for the federal ITC (100% is entered on Line 340, and 20% is subtracted on Line 529). If the contractor is not a taxable supplier, 0% of the contract expenditure qualifies for the ITC. An arm's-length contractor may perform either a standalone SR&ED project or commensurate support work under Paragraph 248(1)(d) that directly supports the payer's Canadian SR&ED. Consequential on the restoration of capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 repealed Subsections 37(14) and 37(15) (the look-through rule that previously required payers to reduce contract and third-party payments by capital expenditures of the performer) effective for property acquired and lease costs payable on or after December 16, 2024.
2. Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345 / Line 541 & Form T1146)

Expenditures incurred for SR&ED performed on the claimant's behalf by a non-arm's-length performer (reported on Line 345) enter the Section 37 pool, but do not qualify directly for the SR&ED ITC in the hands of the payer (100% is subtracted on Line 541 of Part 4). Instead, under Subsection 127(13), the payer and the non-arm's-length performer can jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) together with Form T661 to transfer all or part of the performer's underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures (including the performer's PPA) from the performer (deducted on Line 546) to the payer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool. A partnership cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures on Form T1146 because a partnership is not considered a "person" for purposes of these rules.
3. Third-Party Payments (Line 370, Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) & Form T1263)

A third-party payment (reported on Line 370) is a payment made to an approved association, university, college, research institute, or similar institution (or certain Canadian-resident R&D corporations or agricultural producer check-off organizations) for SR&ED carried out in Canada that is not directly undertaken by or on behalf of the claimant, provided the SR&ED work is related to a business of the claimant and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED. Like arm's-length contracts, 80% of a third-party payment qualifies for the federal ITC (20% is subtracted on Line 529). Claimants are exempt from completing Part 2 of Form T661 for third-party payments, but must complete and attach Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development) for each payment.
5.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)
Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for property acquired—and lease amounts that first become payable—after December 15, 2024:
1. Capital Expenditures Meeting the "All or Substantially All" (ASA ≥90%) Test (Line 390)

Under restored Paragraph 37(1)(b) and Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 (once it becomes available for use under Subsection 37(1.2)) qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 if the claimant intended at acquisition either: (1) to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada; or (2) to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada.
Three strict restrictions govern Line 390 capital expenditures:

items: Used Property Restriction (Regulation 2902(b) / Line 532): Depreciable property that has been used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose prior to its acquisition by the claimant (used equipment) qualifies for the immediate income deduction under Paragraph 37(1)(b), but is a prescribed expenditure under Paragraph 2902(b) of the Regulations and must be subtracted on Line 532 of Part 4 so that it does not qualify for SR&ED ITCs.

Exclusion of Land and Buildings (Paragraphs 37(8)(d) & (e)): Non-depreciable property (such as land, inventory, or goodwill) cannot be claimed. Under Paragraph 37(8)(e), capital expenditures made to acquire a building or a leasehold interest in a building do not qualify as SR&ED expenditures, other than a prescribed special-purpose building under Section 2903 of the Regulations.

40% Refundability on Capital ITCs: For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the enhanced 35% ITC on new ASA capital property within their expenditure limit, Section 127.1 sets the cash refund rate on capital expenditures at 40% (compared to 100% on current expenditures). Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 are deemed by Subsection 37(6) to be CCA allowed to the taxpayer and must not be included on T2 Schedule 8.

body.text: 2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9), Line 504, Part 6C Boxes 788–796)

Under Subsection 127(9), Subparagraph 127(9) "qualified expenditure" (a)(iii), and the SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial work may qualify for partial ITCs as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE). To qualify as first-term SUE, the property must: (a) be depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024; (b) not be General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF); (c) not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (which excludes property intended to be used during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility, plant, or line and intended to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its useful life); (d) be new property (Subparagraph 2902(b)(iii)); and (e) be actually used primarily (more than 50% of its cumulative operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period (starting at acquisition and ending at the end of the first taxation year occurring at least 12 months after acquisition). To qualify as second-term SUE, the property must have qualified as first-term SUE and continue to be actually used primarily (more than 50% of its cumulative operating time) for SR&ED in Canada from acquisition until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition (Second Period).

The qualified expenditure for SUE (claimed on Line 504 and detailed in Part 6C: Box 788 name of property for the 20 most expensive items, Box 790 purchase date, Box 792 25% of capital cost, Box 794 term designation "1" or "2", and Box 796 project numbers) is 25% (1/4) of the capital cost in the first period and an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost in the second period (up to 50% total), determined without borrowed money costs (Section 21) or deemed capital cost adjustments (Subsections 13(7.1) and 13(7.4)), adjusted for non-arm's-length costs (Subsection 127(11.6)), and reduced by related assistance (Subsection 127(18)). SUE capital cost is not added to the Section 37 deductible pool and is instead depreciated under regular CCA rules on T2 Schedule 8.
3. Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024; Lines 350, 355, and Box 759)

Under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 2026), current lease payments first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 for the use of, or right to use, equipment (reported by project in Box 759 of Part 6A, equalling Lines 350 + 355 in Part 3) qualify as follows:

items: Traditional Method (Line 162): If leased equipment is used ASA (≥90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350 (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)). If leased equipment is used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, a proportional percentage of the lease cost may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 if it is directly related and incremental under Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Paragraph 2900(2)(c).

Proxy Method (Line 160): If leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used ASA (≥90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350 (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)). If leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 355 (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)). Equipment used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED cannot be claimed under the Proxy Method.

Building Rent, Land Leases, Bandwidth, and Software Licences: Whether a contract is a lease or a sale is governed by the legal relationship created by the agreement (Shell Canada Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5669). Building rent is excluded under Paragraph 37(8)(e) (except for Regulation 2903 special-purpose buildings; combined building-and-equipment leases require reasonable allocation). Leasing land after December 15, 2024 is allowable as overhead under the Traditional Method if ASA or directly attributable to SR&ED, but is disallowed under the Proxy Method. Following Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1877), paying for dedicated bandwidth, telephone lines, or mainframe capacity constitutes a lease of equipment and is allowable under the Proxy Method if dedicated to SR&ED and not GPOEF; software licences may qualify as capital or lease expenditures depending on the legal terms.

body.text: 5.6 Regulation 2902 Prescribed Exclusions and ITC Recapture (Subsections 127(27) to (36))

Under Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, prescribed expenditures are excluded from qualified expenditures (subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661) and never earn an ITC, even if deductible under the Traditional Method. Under Regulation 2902(a), prescribed current expenditures include outlays for the general administration or management of a business: (1) administrative salaries/wages and related benefits for personnel whose duties are not ASA directed to SR&ED (except to the extent directly attributable under the Regulations); (2) external legal, accounting, or technical consulting fees paid to third parties for preparing SR&ED claims (Clause 2902(a)(i)(B))—though under the explicit exception in Clause 2902(a)(i)(A), salary or wages paid to the claimant's own employees for preparing SR&ED claims are not prescribed expenditures if directly related and incremental; (3) interest and financing costs under Paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g) (Clause 2902(a)(i)(C)); (4) technical conventions and conference expenses (Clause 2902(a)(i)(F)); (5) entertainment expenses; (6) advertising or selling expenses; (7) dues or fees for membership in a scientific or technical society; (8) fines or penalties; and (9) maintenance and upkeep of premises, facilities, or equipment not attributable to SR&ED.
Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under Subsections 127(27) through 127(36) and the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, a claimant must report an ITC recapture (which is added directly to tax payable) if four conditions are met: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property (such as materials transformed into a prototype/product, or ASA/SUE capital equipment) in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by Subsection 127(36)); (2) the cost of the property was a qualified expenditure; (3) a percentage of that cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC; and (4) the claimant converts the property (or another property incorporating it) to commercial use or disposes of it in the year.

Where property is sold at arm's length, recapture is based on proceeds of disposition; where property is converted to commercial use or transferred to a non-arm's-length party, Paragraph 127(27)(f) (and Subparagraph 127(28)(e)(ii) for partnerships / Paragraph 127(29)(f) for transferred expenditures) uses the fair market value (FMV) of the property. For ASA capital equipment, the CRA uses a notional undepreciated capital cost (UCC) calculation to estimate FMV unless the claimant substantiates a lower value. Under Subsections 127(33) to 127(35), disposing of SR&ED capital property to a non-arm's-length purchaser does not trigger immediate recapture if the purchaser continues to use the property as ASA capital property for SR&ED. Recapture never applies to labour costs, overhead, or the sale/conversion of intellectual property (IP), and by CRA administrative policy (de minimis rule), recapture does not apply if scrap sale proceeds or FMV upon conversion to commercial use is less than 10% of the total cost of the property (or if insurance proceeds on materials consumed do not exceed 10% of cost). Any recaptured ITC is added back to the Section 37 deductible pool in the following taxation year under Paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3).
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory (Yukon) administer R&D tax credits (or R&D grants via the corporate tax system in Alberta). Except for Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered on the AT1 return), the CRA administers all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits on behalf of the provinces and Yukon through the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.

body.text: 6.2 Deep-Dive of Major Provincial Regimes
1. Quebec’s 2025–2026 Paradigm Shift: The CRIC, CDAEIA, C3i, and DICI

In its March 25, 2025 provincial budget (set out in Quebec Finance Bulletin 2025-6), the Government of Quebec enacted a major consolidation of its innovation tax incentives for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Quebec abolished eight prior measures—specifically the tax credits for scientific research and experimental development (the 14% / 30% R&D salary credit), university research or public research centres, private partnership pre-competitive research, fees and dues paid to a research consortium, technological adaptation services, and industrial design—and replaced them with the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (RD-1029.8.CR).

The CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit to all eligible corporations operating a business in Quebec with an establishment there, regardless of corporate size or foreign control, at a two-tier rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 maximum. While Quebec legislation remains harmonized with federal Subsection 248(1) regarding the definition of R&D (with the CRA carrying out the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC also covers eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Quebec. Eligible pre-commercialization activities comprise: (a) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for the purpose of commercializing an innovation; and (b) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials.

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC include: 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work in Quebec; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Quebec; 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity; and property acquisition costs (capital equipment used in the work, excluding a building, land, or a right to use a building or land, and excluding property used under a large investment project tax holiday certificate). The CRIC does not provide a proxy overhead calculation. Before applying the 30% and 20% credit rates, the corporation's qualified expenditures must exceed an applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount under the Quebec personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025) for each employee, adjusted to reflect the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

Quebec corporations must also coordinate the CRIC with three companion provincial innovation incentives. First, Quebec's e-business IT salary tax credit (CDAE, which equals 30% of eligible IT salaries—23% refundable and 7% non-refundable for a fiscal year starting in 2025, compared to 24% + 6% in 2024) is replaced for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025 by the CDAEIA for corporations that integrate artificial intelligence (AI) features in a significant way, requiring an annual Investissement Québec certificate and paying 30% of eligible salary above an exclusion threshold (22% refundable + 8% non-refundable in 2026; 21% + 9% in 2027; and 20% + 10% from 2028, halved in certain non-arm's-length cases). Second, the Investment and Innovation Tax Credit (C3i) provides a fully refundable credit of 15%, 20%, or 25% (depending on regional economic vitality) on manufacturing or processing equipment, computer hardware, and management software costs above $5,000 or $12,500 per property, up to a cumulative $100 million cap over four years; because CRIC and C3i cannot be combined on the same equipment expenditure, claimants must allocate each asset to the credit that yields the highest net recovery. Third, the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DICI) reduces the Quebec corporate income tax rate from 11.5% to 2.0% on the eligible portion of income from commercializing qualifying intellectual property in Quebec.
2. Ontario’s Three-Credit Stack (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC) and Federal Pool Grinding Mechanics

Under the federal Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and Paragraph 37(1)(d) / Subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces both the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and federal qualified SR&ED expenditures (unless the taxpayer formally waives or renounces a non-refundable provincial credit by the filing deadline).

In Ontario, a qualifying CCPC claiming both the 8% refundable OITC (Schedule 566) and the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (Schedule 508) is subject to a two-stage sequential pool reduction. First, the OITC is computed at 8% of qualified Ontario expenditures (including the federal PPA, up to the $3,000,000 expenditure limit). Second, under Ontario rules, eligible Ontario expenditures for the 3.5% ORDTC are reduced by the amount of the OITC and any 20% OBRITC claimed. Thus, on $100.00 of total Ontario SR&ED expenditures (including proxy overhead), the OITC is $8.00, and the ORDTC is 3.5% of ($100.00 − $8.00) = $3.22. Third, for federal SR&ED ITC purposes, both the $8.00 OITC and the $3.22 ORDTC reduce the federal expenditure pool, leaving a twice-reduced federal pool of $100.00 − $8.00 − $3.22 = $88.78. Applying the 35% enhanced federal ITC rate to $88.78 yields $31.07, resulting in a combined federal-Ontario credit of $8.00 + $3.22 + $31.07 = $42.29 per $100.00 of total SR&ED expenditures including proxy overhead (42.29%). For a corporation earning the 15% basic federal ITC and claiming only the 3.5% ORDTC, the once-reduced federal pool is $100.00 − $3.50 = $96.50, yielding a federal ITC of 15% × $96.50 = $14.48 and a combined federal-Ontario credit of $3.50 + $14.48 = 17.98% of total SR&ED expenditures including proxy overhead. Note that an Ontario corporation can waive the OITC or ORDTC in whole or in part by delivering a written waiver with its T2 return on or before 6 months after its taxation year-end (or on an amended return for that year).
7. Interaction with Federal Innovation Grants and Government Assistance Rules
7.1 Statutory Mechanics of Government Assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18)–(20))

Under Subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, "government assistance" means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself (including assistance from a Crown corporation, a foreign government, or indirect government assistance administered through a non-profit organization). Effective December 21, 2012, "non-government assistance" is defined as an amount that would be included in income under Paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without reference to Subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)) as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance for the cost of property or an outlay/expense.

Under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18) to 127(20), government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return for the year must be applied on a project-by-project basis to reduce both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (reported on Lines 429 and 513–518 of Form T661). Under Paragraph 37(1)(d), assistance for one project cannot reduce the Section 37 pool expenditures of another project and can only reduce a project's Section 37 pool contribution to nil (any excess is included in income), whereas under Subsections 127(18) and 127(19), any excess assistance or contract payment not applied in the current year is carried forward to reduce qualified expenditures of that project in subsequent taxation years. Where a member of a related non-arm's-length group has assistance exceeding its project expenditures, Subsection 127(20) requires allocating the excess assistance to other group members using Form T1145 (reported on Line 540 of Form T661).
7.2 Stacking Federal Grants (NRC-IRAP, SIF, and EIP) with SR&ED

Canadian innovators frequently combine retroactive SR&ED tax credits with direct federal R&D grants, subject to an overall government assistance stacking ceiling of 75% of eligible project costs according to federal funding guidelines. The primary federal grant programs interacting with SR&ED are: (1) the National Research Council — Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC-IRAP), which operates on an annual budget of approximately $437 million, pairs incorporated SMEs with an Industrial Technology Advisor (ITA), and provides non-repayable grants covering up to 80% of eligible internal R&D labour costs (with typical project contributions ranging from $75,000 to $1,000,000, a median contribution of $75,000, a maximum up to $10,000,000, and an approval rate of roughly 34% of client firms worked with in 2024–25); (2) the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund, a highly selective program (historically ~6% approval rate) for large-scale strategic R&D projects with a minimum eligible project scale of $10,000,000+; and (3) the Energy Innovation Program (EIP), which provides grants typically ranging from $500,000 to $5,000,000 for clean energy, clean fuels, carbon capture, and grid technology R&D.

When a corporation incurs $100,000 in eligible developer salary expenses and receives $80,000 from an NRC-IRAP grant to cover those salaries, Subsection 127(18) requires deducting the $80,000 grant from the SR&ED expenditure pool so that only the remaining $20,000 out-of-pocket salary (plus the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount calculated on the unreduced $100,000 salary base under Regulation 2900(4) where the Proxy Method is elected) remains eligible to earn the SR&ED ITC. Failing to deduct NRC-IRAP or other grants constitutes double-claiming and triggers CRA audit adjustments, clawbacks, and potential penalties.
7.3 The CAE Inc. Judicial Precedent on Repayable Government Loans (2022 FCA 178)

A crucial judicial precedent governing repayable government R&D funding was established by the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King , 2022 FCA 178 (affirming 2021 TCC 57 / 2021 D.T.C. 1050; leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada denied on May 26, 2023). In CAE Inc., the taxpayer received $250 million in contributions over a five-year period from Industry Canada under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) program (including $57 million in 2012 and $59 million in 2013). Even though the arrangement was an unconditionally repayable, non-forgivable loan requiring CAE to repay 135% of the advances ($337.5 million, representing an annual return of approximately 2.5%) over 15 years, the agreement imposed public policy covenants (such as manufacturing exclusively in Canada and conducting post-secondary R&D in Canada). Applying the principles from Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co., Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc., and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada (2014 FCA 196), the Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal held that because the loan terms were not strictly commercial, the entire loan advances constituted "government assistance" under Subsection 127(9) and Paragraph 12(1)(x), immediately reducing CAE's SR&ED ITC pool under Subsection 127(18) in the years received (and only regenerating SR&ED pool additions and ITCs as principal repayments are made in future years under Paragraph 37(1)(c)).
8. Administration, Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Defence
8.1 Prescribed Forms and the Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline

Under Subsection 37(11), Subsection 37(11.1), and Paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before its statutory SR&ED reporting deadline, which is 12 months after the filing-due date of the claimant's income tax return for the year in which the expenditure was incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end, the SR&ED reporting deadline for a corporation is 18 months after the end of its taxation year (and 17.5 months after year-end for individuals). Zero extensions are permitted. If Form T661 is filed after the 18-month reporting deadline, the expenditures are not considered SR&ED expenditures, cannot be deducted under Section 37, and cannot earn any ITC under Section 127. If Form T661 is filed on time, but Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals/trusts) is filed after the 18-month reporting deadline, the allowable SR&ED expenditures can still be included in the Section 37 deductible pool, but the claimant will not earn any ITC on those expenditures.
