body.text: Under Paragraph 37(11)(b), Part 9 of Form T661 requires prescribed information for each claim preparer that has accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim. While Part 9 information is not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline and an SR&ED claim will not be disallowed solely because Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable. Additionally, under the Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), incomplete or inaccurate submissions may lead to monetary penalties.
8.2 The New Pre-Claim Approval Program (Launched April 1, 2026 via Form T1322)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval process using Form T1322 and My Business Account. Under this program, eligible businesses can obtain formal CRA approval of technical project eligibility before work begins or costs are incurred (it cannot be used retroactively as a year-end remedy) for a period of up to three years. Pre-claim approval does not replace the annual filing of Form T661; rather, the claimant reports its pre-claim approval case number on the updated Form T661 (alongside Canadian Research and Development Classification, CRDC, codes). Whereas standard refundable SR&ED claims have a processing service standard of 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (which the CRA aims to meet 90% of the time), a claim consisting of projects granted Pre-Claim Approval that requires only an expenditure review is generally processed within 90 calendar days (unless the actual project carried out differed significantly from what was approved or non-pre-approved projects are included).
8.3 CRA Audit Procedures (RTAs and FRs), Administrative Review, and Appeals

Claims selected for review via risk assessment or random sampling cannot be withdrawn once selected, because Part 10 of Form T661 is a certified declaration that cannot be revoked. Technical eligibility is reviewed by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who reports to a Research and Technology Manager, RTM), while expenditure eligibility is reviewed by a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who reports to a Financial Review Manager, FRM). Most reviews are conducted digitally via videoconferencing (with on-site visits considered on an exceptional basis) and involve interviews with the personnel who performed or directly supervised the work and inspection of contemporaneous evidence. At the end of the review, if adjustments or penalties are proposed, the CRA issues an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and a proposal letter, affording the claimant 30 days to submit written representations before a final decision letter and Notice of Assessment or Reassessment are issued.

If a claimant has concerns during the review, it follows the CRA's three-step dispute resolution process: (1) communicating directly with the RTA or FR; (2) escalating to the RTM or FRM; and (3) requesting an Administrative Review after receiving the proposal package (which verifies adherence to SR&ED legislation, policies, and due process, rather than conducting a second technical review by a new team). Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 days from the date of the notice to file a formal Notice of Objection online via My Business Account / Represent a Client or by mail using Form RC592. A "large corporation" (total taxable capital employed in Canada over $10 million at year-end for the corporation and related corporations) must reasonably describe each issue, specify the exact dollar relief sought for each issue, and pay 50% of the disputed amount while the objection or Tax Court of Canada appeal is pending.
9. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents
9.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC) — The Foundational Five-Question Test

Delivered by Judge Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada on May 1, 1998, Northwest Hydraulic established the foundational five-criteria judicial test for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under Subsection 248(1): (1) Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (2) Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty (involving observing the subject matter, formulating a clear objective, identifying the uncertainty, formulating hypotheses, and methodical testing)? (3) Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? (4) Did the process result in a technological advancement? and (5) Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept, as the work progressed? These five criteria were formally endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (2002 D.T.C. 6740), building upon Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 D.T.C. 1363 and RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA).
9.2 Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 — Defining "Routine Engineering," "Hypothesis," and Contemporaneous Records

In Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC 6), Justice Sommerfeldt established four critical legal definitions regularly applied by the Tax Court. First, at paragraph 17, the Court held that while there is no single statutory definition of "routine engineering," the term typically "describes techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field". Second, at paragraph 26, the Court defined a "hypothesis" as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial". Third, at paragraph 33, the Court summarized the three objective principles characterizing the scientific method: (1) trained and systematic observation; (2) measurement and experiment; and (3) the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, at paragraph 46 (alongside Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313), the Court noted that a written contemporaneous record of hypotheses tested and results kept is not an absolute, mandatory statutory condition to recognize SR&ED, though contemporaneous documentation helps resolve factual disputes.
9.3 Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42 — Prohibiting Component Fragmentation

In Formadrain Inc. (2017 TCC 42), involving a cured-in-place pipe liner and mandrel project, Justice D’Auray rejected the Minister's overly narrow review that attempted to isolate the mandrel project into individual component tasks, holding that the project must be assessed holistically in the context of the combined material and mechanical constraints the company was attempting to resolve. Formadrain successfully substantiated its claim with contemporaneous documentary evidence detailing tests, dates, participants, durations, photographs, objectives, hypotheses, uncertainties, materials used, and results.
9.4 Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47) — Binding Status of Northwest Hydraulic and Expert Witness Gatekeeping

In Kam-Press Metal Products (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. (2022 FCA 72, affirming 2020 TCC 47), the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed that the five-part test in Northwest Hydraulic remains the binding legal interpretation of Subsection 248(1) and that the CRA's 2021 "Why" and "How" guidelines still require underlying methodological rigour. In National R&D Inc., the FCA rejected the appellant's attempt to argue via an article in its book of authorities that the "engineering method" differs from the "scientific method," holding that any methodological distinction in applied sciences must be established through trial evidence. Furthermore, the FCA upheld the Tax Court's refusal to qualify the appellant's proposed independent expert witness because the taxpayer's president had written 65% of the expert's report, the report was an exercise in advocacy rather than an impartial assessment, and the report improperly opined on the ultimate legal question of whether the project qualified as SR&ED.
9.5 Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159 (2025) — Novel Context of Known Substances and Practical Record-Keeping

In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. (2024 TCC 159), the appellant sought to control microbial growth and prevent exploding cans in a room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar-based drink containing cold-pressed juice without using heat pasteurization. After standard preservatives (potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate) turned the beverage milky and spoiled the taste, the appellant hypothesized and tested Chiber (a natural white button mushroom extract produced by Chinova Bioworks). Distinguishing Canafric Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2023 TCC 108), Justice Scott Bodie held that even though Chiber was a commercially available preservative, food scientists had previously used it only in dairy products and never in a canned, cold-pressed juice beverage; applying a publicly available solution in a specific technical context where it has never been used before cannot be resolved by routine engineering and establishes genuine technological uncertainty. Justice Bodie also confirmed that contemporaneous documentation is meant to allow the researchers conducting the work to keep track of hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained to facilitate follow-up action, and does not need to be designed for an outsider unfamiliar with the project to decipher or replicate.

body.text: Walkthrough 2: Quebec Corporation Claiming R&D and Pre-Commercialization Under the New CRIC Plus Federal SR&ED

Consider a qualifying CCPC operating in Montreal, Quebec, for its taxation year running January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 (subject to the post-March 25, 2025 CRIC regime). During 2026, it incurs: (a) $1,200,000 in direct Quebec SR&ED salaries for 10 full-time non-specified R&D engineers (100% SR&ED time); (b) $200,000 in direct Quebec salaries for 2 full-time specialists (100% time) conducting regulatory validation testing and product aesthetics/design for initial certification in conjunction with the Quebec R&D (eligible pre-commercialization under CRIC, ineligible for federal SR&ED); and (c) $200,000 paid to an arm's-length Quebec SR&ED subcontractor.

items: Quebec CRIC Calculation (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T): Gross CRIC qualified expenditures equal $1,200,000 (R&D wages) + $200,000 (pre-commercialization wages) + 50% of the Quebec subcontractor (50% × $200,000 = $100,000) = $1,500,000 (of which $1,300,000 or 86.667% relates to core SR&ED and $200,000 or 13.333% relates to pre-commercialization). For 12 full-time eligible employees, using the $18,571 statutory basic personal amount benchmark from 2025 (12 × $18,571 = $222,852), since $222,852 exceeds the $50,000 floor, the exclusion threshold is $222,852. Net CRIC expenditures above the threshold equal $1,500,000 − $222,852 = $1,277,148. Applying 30% on the first $1,000,000 ($300,000) and 20% on the remaining $277,148 ($55,430) yields a 100% refundable Quebec CRIC of $355,430.

Federal SR&ED Calculation (Form T661 & T2 Schedule 31 under Proxy Method): Only the portion of the Quebec CRIC attributable to core SR&ED ($1,300,000 ÷ $1,500,000 × $355,430 = $308,039) reduces the federal SR&ED pool under Subsection 127(18). Gross federal qualified SR&ED expenditures equal $1,200,000 (Line 300 wages) + $660,000 (55% PPA on Line 502) + $160,000 (80% of the $200,000 arm's-length subcontractor) = $2,020,000. Subtracting the $308,039 SR&ED portion of the CRIC on Line 513 leaves $1,711,961 in net federal qualified expenditures, which at the 35% enhanced refundable rate generates $599,186 in federal cash refunds.

Total Combined Cash Refund: Combining the $355,430 refundable Quebec CRIC and the $599,186 refundable federal SR&ED ITC yields $954,616 in total cash refunds on $1,600,000 of total out-of-pocket R&D and pre-commercialization outlays.

body.text: 11. Senior Technical Auditor’s Compliance Checklist

items: Verify Corporate Status and Phase-Out Election (Post-December 15, 2024 Rules): Confirm whether the claimant qualifies as a CCPC or an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) (or ≥90% ECPC subsidiary). For CCPCs whose prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, model the alternative three-year average consolidated gross revenue phase-out calculation and file the annual election if gross revenue yields a higher expenditure limit toward the $6,000,000 ceiling.

Audit the Cutoff Date for Capital Property and Equipment Leases (December 16, 2024): Verify acquisition and "available for use" dates (Subsection 37(1.2)) for all depreciable capital equipment (Line 390), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504 / Part 6C), and equipment lease payments (Lines 350/355 / Box 759) to ensure no pre-December 16, 2024 capital acquisitions or lease obligations are included. Confirm that any used equipment claimed on Line 390 is subtracted on Line 532 as a Regulation 2902(b) prescribed expenditure so it is deducted only under Section 37 and excluded from Section 127 ITCs.

Validate Specified Employee Caps Using the Correct CPP YMPE (Not YAMPE): Identify all employees owning ≥10% of any class of shares (or not dealing at arm's length with the corporation). Ensure all bonuses and profit-based remuneration are stripped from Line 305, verify that direct SR&ED wages do not exceed 5 × YMPE ($356,500 for 2025; $373,000 for 2026), and ensure Part 5 PPA salary base inclusions do not exceed the lesser of 75% of total base salary or 2.5 × YMPE ($178,250 for 2025; $186,500 for 2026), filing Form T1174 where specified employees work across associated corporations.

Reconcile Subcontractors, Taxable Supplier Status, and Non-Arm's-Length Transfers: Confirm that all Line 340 arm's-length contractors are Canadian taxable suppliers performing work inside Canada and that the 20% reduction is applied on Line 529. For any non-arm's-length R&D contracts on Line 345, verify that 100% is deducted on Line 541 and that a signed Form T1146 is filed on time to transfer the performer's underlying un-marked-up qualified expenditures to the payer.

Track 180-Day Payment Proofs for Accrued Wages and Current Expenses: Cross-check year-end accrued bonuses (for non-specified employees), vacation pay, and subcontractor payables against payment records for the 180-day period following year-end (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26)). Any amount unpaid at day 180 must be reported on Line 315 or Line 520 within the original 18-month reporting deadline to preserve future ITC eligibility when paid.

Account for All Government Assistance, Concessional Loans, and Provincial Credits: Deduct all federal/provincial grants (such as NRC-IRAP), concessional government loans (CAE Inc., 2022 FCA 178), and provincial R&D tax credits received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received by the filing-due date on a project-by-project basis under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(18). In Quebec, segregate pre-commercialization expenditures eligible under the new CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T) from core SR&ED expenditures.

Structure Part 2 Narratives Around the "Why" and "How" Requirements and Preserve Contemporaneous Evidence: Frame every Form T661 Part 2 technical narrative to articulate the specific limitation in available scientific or technological knowledge (distinguishing it from routine engineering per Joel Theatrical Rigging and Manning Canning), the explicit hypotheses formulated, the chronological experiments/analyses conducted, and the logical conclusions reached, backed by dated commit logs, test sheets, photographs, and trial records created as the work progressed.

Enforce the 18-Month Statutory Filing Calendar and Complete Part 9 Disclosures: Calendar the corporate 18-month reporting deadline (and consider Form T1322 Pre-Claim Approval before initiating major new R&D projects). Ensure Form T661, T2 Schedule 31, T2 Schedule 49, and all provincial schedules are filed prior to the deadline, with complete Part 9 claim preparer information to avoid the $1,000 joint-and-several penalty under Subsection 162(5.1).
